Two exercises drawn from the Android Debug Bridge slides. First, you learn to launch any app component using adb shell am with intent actions and data URIs. Then you watch RAM grow and shrink as a foreground service runs, gets killed, and is restarted.

1. Background — what is the Activity Manager?

Inside Android, every running window is an Activity. Every always-on background task is a Service. Every "an event happened" delivery is a Broadcast. All three are managed by one system service — the Activity Manager (am). Through ADB you can tell am to start, stop, broadcast, and inspect everything it manages, with all the privileges that the shell user holds.

The am commands you'll use today follow one of two shapes:

Explicit intent — name the component

adb shell am start -n <package>/<.Component>
adb shell am startservice

android.media.action.STILL_IMAGE_CAMERASystem action that any installed camera app can declare it handles. The OS shows the chooser if more than one matches.


android.media.action.VIDEO_CAPTURESame family — but specifically asks the camera app to start in video mode.


android.intent.action.VIEW -d geo:32.0833,34.8167VIEW is the most generic display intent; the URI scheme decides what type of "view". geo: resolves to the map app.


android.intent.action.SENDTO -d sms:658765SENDTO means "open a composer for this destination, don't send yet". The sms: scheme tells Android the target is an SMS; 658765 after the colon is the destination number.

Deep Link Drill — Day 3 — Android Security Course





Deep Link Drill — Custom URI schemes can send your SMS


A "deep link" is just a URL the app's manifest claims it can handle. When the user taps a link with that scheme, Android resolves the matching app and hands it the URL — including any data sitting in the path or query. This drill shows how a malicious app can use an innocent-looking deep link to fire off SMS messages on the user's behalf.



What you'll learn


    
  
  • How intent-filters in the manifest declare which URLs an app responds to.
    • 
  
  • Why custom schemes (smssender://) aren't owned by anyone — multiple apps can claim them.
    • 
  
  • How an app holding SEND_SMS can be wired to send a message just because the user clicked an HTML link.
    • 
  
  • How to reproduce the same behaviour from adb shell am start without any HTML at all.
    • 




1. Background — what is a deep link?



An ordinary HTTP URL points to a web page. A deep link uses a URI scheme that one or more native apps register for — instead of opening a browser, Android dispatches the URL to the app whose intent-filter matches. The receiving Activity gets the URL via getIntent().getData() and parses out the bits it cares about (numbers in the path, fields in the query, etc.).



The trust model: Android assumes that opening a URL is a safe operation. The browser and the OS shell follow that assumption; they tap-to-open without confirming. So if the app on the receiving end of the deep link does something dangerous with the URL contents — like sending SMS — the dangerous thing happens silently the moment the user taps the link.

Deep Link Drill — Solutions


All commands and URLs are taken from slides 41–42 of Android Application.pptx.



Solution — both methods





Method A: HTML link tapped from the file browser


The bundled test.html at the course folder root contains an input field and a link generator. The runtime-generated link looks like:


smssender://send?data=<number>:<urlencoded-message>


Push the file once, then open from the phone:


adb push test.html /sdcard/Download/test.html
# on the phone: Files app → Download → test.html → fill in fields → tap link



Method B: ADB directly (no HTML)


adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "smssender://send?data=0506944922:hello"

# with a space-and-ampersand-bearing message:
adb shell am start -a android.intent.action.VIEW -d "smssender://send?data=+972506944922:Hello%20%26%20Welcome"





What's inside the URL





PieceRole


smssenderCustom scheme. The DeepLinkApp manifest registers an intent-filter with <data android:scheme="smssender" /> on its launch activity. Any app can register any scheme.


sendHost portion. The intent filter matches android:host="send"; another path on the same scheme could route to a different feature.


?data=...Query string. The app's activity reads getIntent().getData().getQueryParameter("data") in code.


: (in the data value)An app-specific separator chosen by the developer. Everything before : is the destination number; everything after is the message body. Note this is part of the value — the URL parser doesn't interpret it.


%20 / %26URL-encoding for space and ampersand
